original_value: Direct to consumer genetic testing (DTCGT) services where users can identify their inherited diseases and traits, find genetic relatives, and learn more about their ethnic heritage continue to grow in popularity. At the same time, one's DNA is one of the most identifiable, immutable forms of personal information, and sharing it carries risks to one's privacy. What motivates individuals to engage in DTCGT, and what are the implications for information privacy at both the individual and societal levels? This study uses qualitative interviews with ten customers of the DTCGT service 23andMe to explore why they engaged in DTCGT, the benefits they received, their expectations of privacy, and perceptions of risk. It also introduces the use of social exchange theory as a theoretical framework for examining the social dimensions of information privacy and personal disclosure. The findings demonstrate that the participants' assumptions of anonymity, as well as their their belief that their contributions to online genetic databases aid the public good, were key motivating factors. The participants were generally unaware of the potential risks to their individual genetic privacy as well as the impact of large scale genetic testing databases on networked, collective privacy. The findings demonstrate that framework of social exchange theory aids in understanding how the form of the relationship affected the participants' decisions to disclose their personal information to 23andMe as well as their perceptions of risk in the DTCGT context.

result.paraphrase: Direct-to-consumer genetic testing (DTCGT) services, which let users discover inherited diseases and traits, locate genetic relatives, and learn more about their ethnic heritage, continue to gain popularity. At the same time, DNA is among the most identifiable and unchangeable forms of personal information, so sharing it poses privacy risks. What leads people to use DTCGT, and what does this mean for information privacy at both the individual and societal levels? This study draws on qualitative interviews with ten customers of the DTCGT service 23andMe to examine why they participated, the benefits they gained, their privacy expectations, and how they perceived risk. It also proposes social exchange theory as a framework for analyzing the social dimensions of information privacy and personal disclosure. The findings show that assumptions of anonymity, along with the belief that contributing to online genetic databases serves the public good, were major motivating factors. Participants were generally unaware of the possible risks to their own genetic privacy and of how large-scale genetic testing databases affect networked, collective privacy. The findings also show that social exchange theory helps explain how the nature of the relationship influenced participants’ decisions to disclose personal information to 23andMe and their perceptions of risk in the DTCGT context.
